title.analysis: Authentic title "The Psychology of Why You Can't Save" is a second-person diagnosis that presumes the viewer cannot save and promises an explanatory "psychology of" answer. It has no number, stakes or capitalised emphasis. The transcript delivers the explanation (present bias, loss aversion, mental accounting, social comparison, willpower, future self) but only brief solutions. Most nearest peers use concrete objects or numbers ($1,000, $50k, $70K/Year, 30 by 2030, a "Beater"); this abstract psychology frame sits at a WEAK 0.39625 ratio. Association only; no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.opening_words: Have you ever wondered why saving money feels like trying to hold water in your bare hands? You know, you should be putting money aside. You've read all the advice about emergency funds and retirement planning, but somehow your bank account balance keeps hovering around the same disappointing number month after month. Well, here's something that might shock you. The reason you can't save money isn't because you lack willpower or because you're financially
script.ending_words: you've never met. So, there you have it. Your brain isn't sabotaging your savings because it hates you or because you're financially doomed. It's just doing what it was designed to do millions of years ago. The good news. Once you understand that you're not fighting against willpower or discipline, but against evolution itself, you can finally stop beating yourself up and start building systems that actually work.
script.analysis: Full 20001 canonical characters read. A non-blaming explanatory essay: the hook absolves the viewer ("not willpower") and promises advice contrary to tradition. It moves through five biases, each with an evolutionary-mismatch explanation and vivid analogies (water in hands, Stone Age computer, sports car on bicycle brakes, fish climbing a tree). The closing advice — automate, change the environment, choose peers — is brief and mainstream, a payoff gap against the contrarian hook. There are no figures beyond illustrative dollar amounts, so verification is psychological. The McClure 2004 neural dissociation is supported at abstract level. The future-self study is distorted (no one was shown scans of their future self). Ego depletion is presented as settled despite a near-zero multilab replication. The disposition effect and mental accounting are consistent with the literature but not fetched. The stored text garbles "ventral striatum" and misspells Thaler.
beat_map: Hook: saving like holding water; not willpower; brain wired against you; subscribe ask; contrarian promise.
Evolutionary mismatch framing: survival brain, Stone Age computer.
Present bias: $20 now vs $25 later; immediate-reward vs prefrontal systems; sports car/bicycle brakes; $500 retirement vs gadget.
Loss aversion: losses about twice gains; saving coded as loss; avoiding stocks; disposition effect.
Mental accounting: Thaler; found vs earned $100; tax refunds and windfalls.
Recap of three forces; "wait, there's more".
Social comparison: tribal status, social-media highlight reels, keeping up with the Joneses.
Bandwagon effect, group spending spiral and guilt around saving.
Willpower myth: depletion, decision fatigue, industry blame.
Systems over willpower: automation, environment design, peer choice.
Future self: future money as abstract, future self as stranger.
Close: not your fault but evolution; build systems.

claim_audit.assessment: ERSNER2009: participants rated their current and future selves during fMRI. Individual differences in rACC activation between current and future self predicted temporal discounting a week later. People were not shown 'brain scans of their future selves', and the abstract supports individual differences, not universal stranger-equivalence. Distorted.

topic.analysis: Behavioral economics of household saving: present bias, loss aversion, mental accounting, social comparison and bandwagon norms, self-control and future-self continuity, resolved into automation and environment design.
topic.audience_problem: People who intend to save but repeatedly fail and look for a non-blaming explanation plus a workable system.
topic.time_sensitivity: Low; evergreen psychology. Research vintages (2004, 2009, 2016 replication) matter more than news timing.
topic.narrative_angle: "It's not your fault, it's evolution" absolution arc, from bias catalogue to systems.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Test an original behavioral-saving video that grades each bias by evidence strength (e.g. ego depletion failed a 23-lab replication; present-bias neural evidence is abstract-level) and pairs each with one concrete countermeasure the viewer can set up during the video (automatic transfer, commitment device, separate goal account).
topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test

An abstract psychology frame, the absence of numbers or stakes, and a weak solution payoff are plausible but unestablished contributors. The STRONG peer is a concrete contrarian money move.
